clue.text: Fat boy swallowing last of burger

indicators.note: swallowing is eating, so the boy word takes the letter that follows inside itself

parts.note: a lad is a boy

indicators.note: last of asks for only the final letter of the word that follows it

explanation.surface: An overweight lad gulps down the final mouthful of his hamburger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' poses as an adjective describing the boy but is the noun being defined. 'swallowing' puts a letter inside LAD; 'last of' picks the final letter of burger.
explanation.definitionFit: Lard is rendered pig fat used in cooking, so it is one example of a fat.

clue.text: Stir caldron regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so take every second letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A recipe tells the cook to give the pot a turn at steady intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stir' looks like a cook's instruction but is a noun meaning a fuss. 'regularly' takes every second letter of caldron, a variant spelling of cauldron.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, a stir is a commotion or fuss, a synonym of this old word for bustle and bother.

clue.text: Scavenger beginning to drag short bar

indicators.note: beginning to asks for only the opening letter of the word that follows it
short means cut short, so the word for a bar loses its final letter

parts.note: an ingot is a bar of cast metal, such as gold

explanation.surface: A scrap collector starts to haul away a stubby metal rod.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to' takes the first letter of drag; 'short' trims INGOT, a bar of cast metal, to INGO. The dingo, Australia's wild dog, eats carrion as well as hunting.
explanation.definitionFit: The dingo, Australia's wild dog, feeds on carrion and scraps as well as live prey, so it is an example of a scavenger.

clue.text: Reptile got policeman on the toilet

indicators.note: on sets one word directly against the other, here in the order the clue gives them

parts.note: copper is British slang for a police officer
the head, or heads, is naval slang for a ship's toilet

explanation.surface: A snake caught a police officer at his most vulnerable, sitting in the lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' just joins two slang words in the order given: British slang for a police officer, then sailors' slang for a ship's lavatory. The answer is a venomous American snake.
explanation.definitionFit: A copperhead is a venomous North American pit viper, and every snake is a reptile.

clue.text: Gas and water required to live in French manor

parts.note: to gas is to talk idly at length, which is to chat

parts.words: water required to live in French
parts.note: eau is the French word for water, the liquid every living thing needs

explanation.surface: Anyone moving into a grand country house in France needs the utilities connected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' belongs to the wordplay, turning water into EAU, so 'manor' alone is the definition. 'Gas' is the verb meaning to chatter, not the household fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: A chateau is a large country house or castle in France, the counterpart of an English manor house.

clue.text: Dilly-dallying drawn in a strip cartoon

indicators.note: drawn can mean pulled or dragged about, so the letters of the four words after it are pulled into a new order

parts.note: these four words supply the fifteen letters

explanation.surface: Someone's dithering is depicted in a newspaper comic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawn' looks like the cartoonist's work but is the anagram signal: the fifteen letters of IN A STRIP CARTOON are pulled into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: To dilly-dally is to waste time putting things off, and this is the formal noun for such habitual delay.

clue.text: Thrilled to have gone out without cold

indicators.note: without is used in its old sense of outside, so the going-out word wraps around the letter that follows

parts.note: exited means gone out, left
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted to have been outdoors and not caught a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but is the old word for 'outside', as in 'within and without', so EXITED wraps round C. 'to have' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe someone stirred up with eager pleasure, so they are close synonyms.

clue.text: After touring Haiti mule is put down

indicators.note: touring is travelling around, so after their tour the letters of the next two words stand in new places

parts.note: these two words supply the nine letters

explanation.surface: Once its trek round a Caribbean country is over, a pack animal is destroyed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put down' reads as destroying a sick animal, but it means to belittle. 'After touring' is the anagram signal: the letters of HAITI MULE change places.
explanation.definitionFit: To put someone down is to belittle or shame them, a synonym of this verb.

clue.text: A perfect example with note used in thorough contract

indicators.note: used in says the example and its note are placed inside the word for thorough

parts.note: arrant means thorough or out-and-out, as in an arrant fool
a gem is a perfect example of its kind
E is a note of the musical scale and N abbreviates note, but the clue has only one note where two are needed

explanation.surface: A model specimen and its memo are cited in a comprehensive legal agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is faulty: 'used in' puts the example and its note inside the word for thorough, but that spells only ARRANGEMET, an N short. The paper's puzzles editor admitted his edit broke it; 'notes' (E plus N) would have worked.
explanation.definitionFit: A contract is a formal agreement between parties, and an agreement of that kind is one sense of the answer.

clue.text: Leave coin for the Australian resident

parts.note: to go is to leave
the anna was a small coin of British India, worth a sixteenth of a rupee

explanation.surface: Someone is told to put down some change for a person living down under.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'resident' is no person: a goanna is a large Australian monitor lizard. ANNA, an old Indian coin worth a sixteenth of a rupee, is a setters' favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A goanna is a large monitor lizard native to Australia, so it is whimsically one of that country's inhabitants.

clue.text: Cameron is nervous with answer being filmed

indicators.note: someone nervous is jittery and unsettled, so the letters of the name before it are shaken into a new order

parts.note: the name supplies the seven letters to rearrange
A is the abbreviation for answer, as in Q and A

explanation.surface: A politician named Cameron gets jittery about replying while the cameras roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is nervous' is the anagram signal, and the jumble is slight: the name's last two letters simply move to the front. The surface evokes David Cameron, Britain's prime minister when the puzzle ran in 2013.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a person in shot while a recording is made, which is the state of being filmed.

clue.text: Junk beats our destroyer

indicators.note: to junk something is to scrap it, so as a command it tells you to break up and rebuild the letters that follow

parts.note: these two words supply the eight letters

explanation.surface: A Chinese sailing boat proves more than a match for our navy's warship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Junk' reads as the Chinese sailing boat but is an instruction to scrap and rebuild BEATS OUR. The 'destroyer' is a person who wrecks things, not a warship.
explanation.definitionFit: A saboteur deliberately wrecks machinery or plans, so is someone who destroys things.

clue.text: In short, work with a cook to get booze

indicators.note: short means cut short, so the word for 'in' loses its final letter

parts.note: among means in the midst of, in
to till the soil is to work it
to do a dish is to cook it, as in 'I'll do the fish'

explanation.surface: Put briefly: team up with a chef and you will be given alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' reads as one phrase meaning 'briefly', but the words split: 'In' is a preposition to translate and 'short' cuts off that word's last letter. The answer is a medium-dry Spanish sherry.
explanation.definitionFit: Amontillado is a medium-dry Spanish sherry, and sherry is one example of booze.

clue.text: Skill displayed by man camping?

parts.note: Al, a man's short name, sits inside the word tent: a man in a tent is a man camping

explanation.surface: A fellow on a camping trip shows off his know-how.
explanation.walkthrough: No word says 'put inside': 'camping?' is a whimsical way of saying 'in a tent', so AL, a man, sits inside TENT. The question mark flags the liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: A talent is a natural aptitude or ability, a near-synonym of skill.

clue.text: Threw unsold pens out

indicators.note: out can mean astray or not in its right place, so the letters before it are out of order and must be rearranged

parts.note: these two words supply the ten letters

explanation.surface: A stationer binned the biros that nobody bought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Threw' means baffled, as in 'the question threw me', not hurled. 'out' is the anagram signal for the letters of UNSOLD PENS.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw someone is to baffle or perplex them, and the answer is the past tense of a verb meaning just that.

clue.text: Soon object to being in work

indicators.note: being in says the words for 'object to' are found inside the word for work

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it
to resent something is to object to it, to feel aggrieved by it

explanation.surface: Before long, someone will start to mind having a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being in' is the container signal. The surface reads 'in work' as 'employed', but 'work' is a verb here, as in working at a trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Presently means before long or in a little while, a synonym of soon.

clue.text: Jump with guitar at end of recital

parts.note: axe is musicians' slang for a guitar

indicators.note: end of asks for only the final letter of the word that follows it

explanation.surface: A performer leaps into the air, instrument in hand, as the concert finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: AXE is musicians' slang for a guitar; 'end of' takes the last letter of recital. An axel is a figure-skating jump named after the Norwegian skater Axel Paulsen.
explanation.definitionFit: An axel is a figure-skating leap with one and a half turns in the air, so it is a kind of jump.

clue.text: Blinking tough cause?

parts.note: read it back to front: a cause of tough blinking, a sore swelling on the eyelid that makes every blink hurt

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that a campaign is a jolly hard one to support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blinking' poses as the mild British swear word, as in 'blinking difficult'. Read it literally instead: something that causes blinking to be tough.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, which makes blinking painful and difficult.

clue.text: Cut out alcohol and start to forestall beastly complaint

indicators.note: out means outside here, so the cutting word wraps around the pieces that follow

parts.note: to sever is to cut through or cut off
wine is an alcoholic drink

indicators.note: start to asks for only the opening letter of the word that follows it

explanation.surface: Give up drinking and you begin to head off a nasty illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut out' reads as 'give up', but 'out' means outside, so the cutting word wraps round the drink and the letter 'start to' takes from forestall. 'beastly' is literal: this disease strikes pigs.
explanation.definitionFit: Swine fever is a serious viral disease of pigs, so it is literally an illness of beasts.

clue.text: Caretaker takes note into small room with patients

indicators.note: into says the note is carried inside the letters for a small room, not set beside them

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a ward is a hospital room where patients are cared for
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale, also spelt ti

explanation.surface: A janitor carries a written message into a cramped hospital room full of sick people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' is the container signal; 'takes' only links the definition to the wordplay. The note is the seventh of the sol-fa scale, more often spelt 'ti'.
explanation.definitionFit: A steward looks after and manages a property or estate on someone's behalf, which is a caretaker's job.

clue.text: One in test about carbon left to cry

indicators.note: about means around, so the test word, already holding its extra letter, goes round the two letters that follow
in says the letter for one sits inside the word for a test

parts.note: an exam is a test
I is the Roman numeral for one
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: A candidate in an exam on carbon is abandoned in tears.
explanation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: 'in' puts I inside EXAM (EXAIM), then 'about' wraps that round C and L. 'cry' means call out, not weep; 'to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To exclaim is to call out suddenly with strong feeling, one sense of the verb cry.

clue.text: Rip off a jacket

definitions.meaning: to rip someone off is to swindle or overcharge them
a warm casual jacket made of soft synthetic pile

explanation.surface: Someone tears a coat from their back.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to swindle someone out of money; as a noun it is a soft, warm zip-up top.

clue.text: Meticulous member of the clergy on a cycle

indicators.note: in an across clue a piece that is on another is added to its end, so the clergy word follows the two letters

parts.note: C is an abbreviation for cycle given in Collins English Dictionary, as in c/s for cycles per second
a curate is a junior Anglican cleric who assists a parish priest

explanation.surface: A painstaking vicar pedals along on a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' in an across clue means 'tacked onto the end of', so CURATE follows A and C. C for cycle is a rare dictionary abbreviation (c/s, cycles per second) that solvers found obscure.
explanation.definitionFit: Meticulous work is exact and careful in every detail, which is what accurate also conveys.

clue.text: On public transport a puzzle's the answer!

parts.note: re means on the subject of, concerning
a bus is a form of public transport

explanation.surface: For a dull commute, doing a brainteaser is the solution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' means 'concerning', which is RE, not 'aboard'. The closing words just say a puzzle is what you are looking for; a rebus shows words as pictures and letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebus represents a word or phrase by pictures, letters and symbols, so it is one kind of puzzle.

clue.text: Beef put on butter is prime bit

parts.note: Collins gives 'on or onwards' as a sense of the adverb past: he walked on, he walked past
a ram butts with its head, so whimsically it is a butter

indicators.note: prime can mean first, so the prime bit of the word before it is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A slice of steak laid on a pat of butter is a choice morsel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' is something that butts, a RAM, not the dairy spread. 'on' gives PAST through a rare adverb sense, and 'prime bit' takes the first letter of 'is'. 'put' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastrami is brisket that has been cured, spiced and smoked, so it is a form of beef.

clue.text: Attack from male hiding in a woody plant

indicators.note: hiding in says the letter for male is concealed inside the two-part phrase that follows

parts.note: a bush is a low woody plant, a shrub
M is the abbreviation for male, as on forms

explanation.surface: A man concealed in the shrubbery launches an assault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hiding in' puts M inside A BUSH. The surface all but describes the answer: a surprise attack by someone lying concealed.
explanation.definitionFit: An ambush is a surprise assault launched from a concealed position, so it is a kind of attack.

clue.text: Second explosive novel

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second, the unit of time
HE is the military abbreviation for high explosive

explanation.surface: An author's follow-up book causes a sensation.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a title: H. Rider Haggard's 1887 adventure story, a favourite of setters. HE, for high explosive, is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the title of H. Rider Haggard's 1887 adventure story about an immortal queen, so an example of a novel.

clue.text: Comfortably numb melody is pure metal!

indicators.note: an unusual signal: comfortably can mean easily or loosely, so the letters of the next two words are loosened into a new order

parts.note: these two words supply the ten letters

explanation.surface: A dreamy, anaesthetised tune turns out to be out-and-out heavy rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comfortably' is a rare anagram signal (read it as 'loosely'), chosen to evoke Pink Floyd's song Comfortably Numb: NUMB MELODY is rearranged. 'metal' is the chemical kind, not the music.
explanation.definitionFit: Molybdenum is a chemical element, a hard silvery-white metal, and an element is by nature unalloyed.

clue.text: Petition against introduction of toxic fat

indicators.note: against means right up next to, so the petitioning word is set beside the letter that follows

parts.note: to sue is to petition or appeal, as in suing for peace

indicators.note: introduction of asks for only the opening letter of the word that follows it

explanation.surface: A campaign to stop a harmful grease being brought into our food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Petition' is the verb SUE, not a noun; 'against' sets it beside T, the 'introduction of' toxic. Suet is hard fat from around an animal's kidneys, used in British puddings.
explanation.definitionFit: Suet is the hard white fat from around the kidneys of cattle and sheep, used in cooking.
